results.title: Federated Disentangled Representation Learning for Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection | Albarqouni Lab
results.content: # Federated Disentangled Representation Learning for Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection. Cosmin Bercea, Benedikt Wiestler, Daniel Rueckert, Shadi Albarqouni. Recent advances in Deep Learning (DL) and the increased use of brain MRI have provided a great opportunity and interest in automated anomaly segmentation to support human interpretation and improve clinical workflow. Here, we present FedDis (Federated Disentangled representation learning for unsupervised brain pathology segmentation) to collaboratively train an unsupervised deep convolutional neural network on 1532 healthy MR scans from four different institutions, and evaluate its performance in identifying abnormal brain MRIs including multiple sclerosis (MS), vascular lesions, low-grade tumors (LGG), and high-grade tumors/glioblastoma (HGG/GB) on a total of ~538 scans from 6 different institutions and datasets. We found out that FedDis is especially beneficial for clients that share both healthy and anomaly data coming from the same institute, improving their local anomaly detection performance by up to 227% for MS lesions and 77% for brain tumors.

Code and models are available at Brain Tumor Extraction from MRI Brain Images Using Marker Based Watershed Algorithm * : Benson C CBenson C C * : Lajish V LLajish V L A Local Statistics Based Region Growing Segmentation Method for Ultrasound Medical Images  Abstract— This paper presents the region based segmentation method for ultrasound images using local statistics. Assisted by a novel self-supervision task that exploits the 3D structure of medical images through supervoxels, our proposed anomaly detection-inspired few-shot medical image segmentation model outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on two representative MRI datasets for the tasks of abdominal organ segmentation and cardiac segmentation. A review of deep learning based methods for medical image multi-organ segmentation Deep learning has revolutionized image processing and achieved the-state-of-art performance in many medical image segmentation tasks. Recently proposed Autoencoder-based methods for unsupervised anomaly segmentation in brain MRI have shown promising performance, but face difficulties in modeling distributions with high fidelity, which is crucial for accurate delineation of particularly small lesions. In a range of experiments comparing our method to different State-of-the-Art approaches on three different brain MR datasets with MS lesions and tumors, we show improved anomaly segmentation performance and the general capability to obtain much more crisp reconstructions of input data at native resolution. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method over intensity-based segmentation alone (i.e. Gaussian mixture model) and gradient-based segmentation alone (i.e. distance regularized level set evolution) on grayscale medical image datasets, including the public 3DIRCADb-01 dataset. Among different existing medical image segmentation methods, graph-based approaches are relatively new and show good features in clinical applications.

results.title: Patched Diffusion Models for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Brain MRI | OpenReview
results.content: ## Patched Diffusion Models for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Brain MRIDownload PDF. **Keywords:** Deep Learning, Unsupervised Anomaly Detection, MRI, Diffusion Models. **TL;DR:** We approach unsupervised anomaly detection in brain MRI scans with patch-based diffusion models, utilizing global spatial context to improve the local estimation of anatomically consistent anatomy in MRI scans of healthy brains. **Abstract:** The use of supervised deep learning techniques to detect pathologies in brain MRI scans can be challenging due to the diversity of brain anatomy and the need for annotated data sets. An alternative approach is to use unsupervised anomaly detection, which only requires sample-level labels of healthy brains to create a reference representation. To accomplish this, generative models are needed to create anatomically consistent MRI scans of healthy brains. In this paper, we propose a method that reformulates the generation task of diffusion models as a patch-based estimation of healthy brain anatomy, using spatial context to guide and improve reconstruction.
